title: The Fortune-Teller
subtitle: Machado de Assis (1884) — a woman with a pack of cards, a lover in a hurry, and an ending one sentence long.
crosslink: Need an easier version? Read this story at A2/B1 level →
grammar_tab: Grammar — The Future in the Past
intention: you'll tell a Brazilian story about a prediction and its price, and use the future in the past — would, was going to, was to — to report what people were told would happen, and to hint at what really did.
warmup: Have you ever had your fortune told — cards, palms, stars, a fortune cookie? Did any of it come true?
Why do intelligent people who 'believe in nothing' still read horoscopes?
A friend tells you they are having a secret affair with another friend's wife or husband. What do you say?
vocab_intro: Before we read, let's unlock the words you'll need. Think first — the Reveal only confirms.

vocab.heading: A. Work it out from the sentence
vocab.instruction: Read each sentence aloud and say what the bold word means from the rest of the sentence. Then reveal.

items.sent: It was imprudent to visit such a house in daylight: anyone might see her go in, and her husband might hear of it.
items.meaning: imprudent (adj) — unwise; not thinking about the risks.

items.sent: He scolded her for taking such risks for his sake — and yet he could not help feeling flattered that she had.
items.meaning: flattered (adj) — pleased because someone has shown that they admire or value you.

items.sent: The letter had no signature and no address; it was anonymous, and that made it more frightening.
items.meaning: anonymous (adj) — from a person whose name is not known or not given.

items.sent: He needed a plausible excuse for his absence — something ordinary enough that nobody would question it.
items.meaning: plausible (adj) — seeming reasonable or likely to be true.

vocab.heading: B. Close in meaning, or opposite?
vocab.instruction: Say the word that fits, then reveal.

items.sent: Sceptical is close in meaning to which word — doubting, delighted, or careless?
Perfidious is close in meaning to which word — treacherous, lazy, or generous?
items.meaning: perfidious (adj) ≈ treacherous, deliberately disloyal. A strong, literary word.

items.sent: Puerile is the opposite of which word — mature, cheap, or honest?
items.meaning: puerile (adj) — the opposite of mature: childish, silly. He laughed at his fears, which he now saw were puerile.

vocab.heading: C. Choose the meaning
vocab.instruction: One sentence, three options. Say a, b or c — then reveal.

items.sent: She was most prepossessing: lively, quick, with burning eyes. Prepossessing means: (a) attractive, making a good first impression (b) wealthy (c) suspicious
items.meaning: (a) — prepossessing (adj) — attractive; creating a good impression at once.

items.sent: He feared the anonymous writer would denounce him to the husband. To denounce someone is: (a) to forgive them (b) to publicly accuse or inform against them (c) to introduce them
items.meaning: (b) — to denounce (v) — to accuse publicly or inform on. (noun: denunciation)

items.sent: Their intimacy grew slowly — the same books, the same walks, then a hand held a moment too long. Intimacy is: (a) a business partnership (b) a close personal relationship (c) a quarrel

vocab_use: Sort the ten words into words about character, words about feelings, and words about deception. Say why.
Using anonymous, denounce and plausible, predict what goes wrong in this story.
story_intro: Machado's story in the 1921 English translation, tightly shortened. Read each part; after it, try the quick check from memory, then talk about the question. The ending is one sentence — don't read ahead.

story.title: Part 1 — 'Laugh, laugh'

paras.to: for the home of the card reader.
skip: The day on which he rid himself

check.q: What did the fortune-teller tell Rita, and why does Camillo scold her for going?
check.a: That Rita loved 'a certain person', that she feared he would forget her, and that there were no grounds for the fear. Camillo calls the visit imprudent — her husband Villela might learn of it.

check.q: What does Camillo believe in — and how does he feel about Rita's superstition?
check.a: Nothing: the beliefs his mother gave him disappeared by the time he was twenty. He finds her fear childish, but he is secretly flattered that she takes risks for him.

story.discuss: Rita says the fortune-teller 'guessed everything'. Did she? What could a clever card-reader work out about a nervous, well-dressed married woman who comes alone?

story.title: Part 2 — Three names, one adventure

paras.from: Villela, Camillo and Rita: three names
skip: Into this course there may have entered

check.q: How are the three connected, and what did Villela do for Camillo when Camillo's mother died?
check.a: Villela and Camillo have been friends since childhood; Villela married Rita and moved to the city. When Camillo's mother died, Villela arranged the funeral and the affairs of the estate, and Rita consoled him — they were 'genuine friends'.

check.q: What frightens Camillo into staying away from Villela's house, and what plan do the lovers make?
check.a: Anonymous letters calling him perfidious and saying the affair is known. He stops visiting; when Villela grows grave and silent, they agree to give each other up for several weeks and part in tears.

story.discuss: Machado compares Rita to a serpent 'winding her coils' about Camillo. Who is the narrator blaming — and do you accept it?

story.title: Part 3 — 'Come immediately'

paras.from: On the following day Camillo received at his department
skip: He sought to establish a connection
As he walked it occurred to him to step into
Camillo leaned back in his seat
There was little light, the stairs
And he began to think of a plausible explanation

check.q: Why does Camillo, who believes in nothing, end up climbing the fortune-teller's stairs?
check.a: His carriage is blocked directly outside her house; fear has woken his childhood superstitions, Hamlet's line echoes in him, and he thinks: what could he lose?

check.q: What does the fortune-teller tell him, how much does he pay her, and what happens at Villela's house?
check.a: That he need fear nothing, that 'the third' knows nothing, and that the lovers are safe. He pays ten milreis — five times her usual fee. At the house, Rita lies dead on the sofa and Villela shoots him.

story.discuss: Reread what the fortune-teller actually says. Is there a single thing in it that she could not have read from his face and his clothes? Why does Machado let us see her counting the money?

grammar.h2: The grammar this story runs on: the future in the past
grammar.intro: This is a story about predictions. A fortune-teller says what will happen; the narrator, who knows how it ends, tells us what would happen — and what was to happen. Reporting a prediction from inside the past is a skill of its own.
notes:
1. Reporting predictions — will becomes would.
Direct: "You will be rich." → Reported: The palm-reader said she would be rich.
Also: can → could ("you can relax" → he could relax) · is going to → was going to ("it's going to rain" → they said it was going to rain) · may → might.

2. The narrator's future — would, was going to, was about to.
• "She did not know that in a year she would own the shop." (the story's future, seen from its past)
• "He was going to resign, but the phone rang." (a plan, often not carried out)
• "The train was about to leave." (on the point of)

3. was / were to + verb — fate, destiny, arrangement.
• "The meeting was to begin at ten." (arranged)
• "It was to be his last journey." (destined — the narrator knows)
A cool, formal way to say would; storytellers love it because it sounds inevitable.

exercises.instruction: Turn each thing she said into reported speech. Watch the verb: will → would, can → could, is going to → was going to.
items: "Nothing will happen to you." → She told him that nothing ___ (happen) to him.
"The gentleman is going to receive good news." → She said the gentleman ___ (receive) good news.
"Your fears will disappear." → She promised that his fears ___ (disappear).
"You can go in peace." → She said he ___ (go) in peace.
"The other man knows nothing and will never know." → She assured him the other man ___ (never / know).

exercises.h3: The narrator's future: would, was about to, was to
exercises.instruction: Follow the hint in brackets. Where there is no hint, use would.
items: Camillo did not know that within the hour he ___ (be) dead.
The letter that ___ (be to / change) everything was already on its way.
Rita ___ (be about to / leave) when the card-reader called her back.
Villela had married a woman who ___ (be to / cost) him his peace.
He thought the crisis ___ (come) fast; he was wrong only about how.

exercises.h3: Put it together — the last hour
exercises.instruction: Fill each gap with the form the hint asks for. Read it aloud; notice how the reader knows more than Camillo.
items: The card-reader had said that nothing ___ (happen). Camillo, who ___ (be to / die) that afternoon, believed her. He decided that he ___ (be going to / explain) his absence as a business matter and that the three of them ___ (soon / laugh) about it together. The door ___ (be about to / open) — and the future he had been promised ___ (never / come).
answers: would happen · was to die · was going to explain · would soon laugh (would soon be laughing) · was about to open · would never come

grammar.outro: In the Speak tab, report what the fortune-teller promised with would, and tell the reader what was to happen instead.

deeper.h2: Why this story stays with you
paras: Joaquim Maria Machado de Assis (1839–1908) was the grandson of freed slaves, the son of a house-painter, largely self-taught — and by his death the greatest writer Brazil had produced. He wrote 'A Cartomante' in 1884 for a Rio newspaper, in the years when he had stopped writing romantic novels and started writing cold, funny, merciless ones. Isaac Goldberg's English version appeared in 1921.

The story opens with Hamlet — 'more things in heaven and earth' — and then spends three thousand words demolishing the line. The fortune-teller guesses nothing. She sees a frightened, well-dressed young man who says 'to me and to her', and she tells him what every frightened lover wants to hear; then she eats her raisins and pockets five times her fee. What kills Camillo is not the cards. It is that a man who 'believed in nothing' wanted, for one afternoon, to believe — and it cost him the hour in which he might have run.
deeper.note: Look again at the last sentence. Machado gives the murder one line, no adjectives, no comment. Everything before it was slow. Why does he refuse to slow down at the end?
questions: Villela never speaks after the first scene, and we never see him discover the affair. Is he a monster, a victim, or something the story is not interested in? Why keep him offstage?
The anonymous letters: who wrote them? The narrator hints at 'a violent rival'. Does it matter that we never find out?
Camillo pays ten milreis instead of two, and the narrator tells us her 'eyes sparkled'. What is Machado saying about faith, and about what it costs?
Is this a story against superstition — or against a man who was too proud to have any until he was frightened?

speak.useful: Report the prediction: "She told him that nothing would happen…", "She said the other man was going to…". Tell the reader the truth: "He did not know that he was to…", "He was about to…". For opinions: "What's striking is…", "You could argue that…", "The irony is that…".

tasks.label: Task A · Tell the whole story (4 minutes)
paras: Tell 'The Fortune-Teller' to someone who has never read it. Move through the arc: Rita and the cards → the three friends and how the affair began → the anonymous letters → Villela's note → the blocked street and the stairs → the fortune-teller's promise → the house.

Report the predictions with would and was going to, use was to at least once, and at least five key words (imprudent, flattered, anonymous, plausible, sceptical, perfidious, puerile, prepossessing, denounce, intimacy).

tasks.label: Task B · Who killed Camillo? (4 minutes)
paras: Four candidates: Villela, who pulled the trigger; the fortune-teller, who told him he was safe; Rita, who started it; and Camillo himself, who wanted to believe. Build a case for one of them, then argue for a different one for one minute.

tasks.label: Task C · A prediction (4 minutes)
paras: Tell a story — real, famous or invented — that turns on a prediction: what someone was told would happen, and what was to happen instead. Use the future in the past throughout.
menu: Macbeth, told by the witches that no man born of woman would harm him.
Oedipus, whose parents were told what their son would do — and who did it precisely because they tried to prevent it.
The economist who predicted the crash and was laughed at — until it came.
A horoscope, a fortune cookie or a palm-reading that someone in a film takes far too seriously.
A family superstition — what you were told would happen if you broke it, and whether it ever did.
A weather forecast, a medical prognosis or an election poll that was confidently wrong.

final: Camillo believed in nothing until he was afraid. Is unbelief a conviction, or just a comfortable habit that fear can break?
The fortune-teller is the only person in the story who gets exactly what she wants. Is she the villain, or the only honest professional in it?
If Camillo had not stopped at the house, would he have lived? What is Machado saying about the hour we waste hoping for good news?
Before you go — from memory: report one prediction with would, one with was going to, and make one sentence with was to about a character's fate.
